title: RustingStrata – Pure Rust LLM GGUF Engine, Runs Models > VRAM on CUDA and Vulkan
content:
A pure-Rust inference engine for GGUF models, built for MoE models that do not fit in VRAM. The CUDA kernels are compiled at run time with NVRTC, and the same kernels run on Vulkan: no C++ build step, no ggml. Experts that do not fit in VRAM run on the CPU at the same time as the GPU work, and the expert placement adapts to the routing it sees.
Supported models: Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5/3.6, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Recursive Flint, Gemma 4, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, Hy4-flash, Inkling 2 Mini and Kolibri 1.1. The architectures, the GGUF types and the notes for each model are in docs/MODELS.md.
Version 1.4.0.
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on an RTX 3060 12 GB (Ryzen 5 7600X, 32 GB RAM), CUDA, greedy, against llama.cpp tuned for the same file. Neither file fits in VRAM.
serve --parallel N decodes the requests together in one batched forward (CUDA). Same machine, same load script
(tools/loadtest.py: N streamed chats at once, 128 reply tokens each, greedy), total decode tok/s:
vLLM runs bf16 weights and RustingStrata Q4_K_M, so the dense columns are not like for like. The 27 GB MoE file does not fit on the 12 GB card, so vLLM was not run on it. RustingStrata reads each expert once for all requests of a step, runs the experts that are not in VRAM on the CPU, and keeps slot state that does not fit in VRAM in RAM. The MoE column moves by about 30% between runs on this machine (the 27 GB file is read through a 30 GB page cache).
The method, the ranges, Vulkan, the other models and the quality checks are in docs/BENCHMARKS.md.
Windows (PowerShell; installs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\RustingStrata, adds it to PATH and makes a Start menu
entry that opens the chat page):
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RustingStudio/RustingStrata/main/install.ps1 | iex
Linux x86_64 (installs to ~/.local/bin):
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RustingStudio/RustingStrata/main/install.sh | sh
Arch Linux: yay -S rustingstrata-bin (AUR). Or download a binary from the
releases page, or build it (Rust 2024 edition; on Windows
install the Visual Studio C++ Build Tools first):
cargo build --release    # the binary is target/release/rustingstrata
Then rustingstrata serve --gpu --open opens the chat page, which downloads models, and rustingstrata interface
asks a few questions in the terminal. rustingstrata update replaces the binary with the newest release (--check
only says whether one is out); serve prints a line at start when a newer release is out. A binary installed by a
package manager (the AUR package) is updated with that package manager.
A GPU run needs one of:
- an NVIDIA driver with the CUDA NVRTC library (loaded at run time). Volta (sm_70), Turing (sm_75) and Ampere or newer
(sm_80+) work; CUDA 13 dropped Volta, so a V100 needs the 12.x toolkit. Pascal and older use Vulkan.
The library is found by name (libnvrtc.so; on Windows nvrtc64_130_0.dll or nvrtc64_120_0.dll, on PATH or
under %CUDA_PATH%\bin); STRATA_NVRTC names another file. Without it the run falls back to Vulkan.
- a Vulkan 1.3 driver with shaderFloat64, int8/16/64 and subgroup size 32 or a fixed 64 (tested on RTX 3060, Radeon VII and V100; Intel Arc lacks shaderFloat64).
- for --backend hip: a ROCm runtime with hiprtc (libamdhip64.so, libhiprtc.so), also loaded at run time; the
kernels are compiled for the card's gfx target on first use. Experimental — status, numbers and limits are in
docs/HIP.md.
--gpu picks CUDA when it loads, else Vulkan; --backend chooses (cuda, vulkan or hip). The first CUDA run compiles the kernels (~15 s) and
caches them. Every GPU tried so far is in docs/SUPPORTED_GPUS.md.
Run rustingstrata with no arguments (double-click rustingstrata.exe on Windows). It starts a server on
http://127.0.0.1:8080 and opens a chat page that downloads models from Hugging Face and switches between the ones in
your models folder. Any app that takes an OpenAI-compatible address (Open WebUI, Jan, SillyTavern, code editors) can
use http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1.
rustingstrata interface asks for the model, the mode (terminal chat, chat page, API server, speed test), GPU or CPU,
the context length and the address, prints the command these make and runs it.
With flags:
M=path/to/model.gguf
rustingstrata calibrate --model $M --dry-run  # preview the workload matrix and knob space
rustingstrata calibrate --model $M     # once per model and machine: best chunk, MTP drafts, short threshold
rustingstrata chat --model $M --gpu    # --think for thinking mode, --temp 0.7 to sample
rustingstrata generate --model $M --gpu --prompt "Write a haiku about rivers." -n 128
rustingstrata serve --model $M --gpu --addr 127.0.0.1:8080
rustingstrata bench --model $M --gpu --pp 512,4096 --tg 128
Without --gpu the model runs on the CPU reference, which is slow and meant for checking. DeepSeek, GLM, Hy4 and
Inkling 2 open the GPU by themselves.
- USAGE.md: flags, the chat page and MCP tools, the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, prompt caching, several GPUs.
- CALIBRATION.md: the budgeted search, task corpora, the spec sweep and the JSON file.
- MODELS.md: supported architectures and GGUF types, notes and caveats for each model.
- BENCHMARKS.md: every model against llama.cpp; older runs are in the benchmark history.
- HOSTING.md: running a server for other people.
- SUPPORTED_GPUS.md and AMD.md: the GPUs tried so far and AMD notes.
- VISION.md: image input. LORA.md: LoRA adapters.
- ROADMAP.md: what is planned next, by section; ideas from users are welcome.
cargo test --release                      # GPU tests need the model: STRATA_MODEL=path/to/model.gguf
python -I tools/parity.py $M --extra "--gpu" --tag gpu   # agreement with llama.cpp (needs llama-server once)
CI only builds, so run the tests before a pull request.
Source map: src/gguf.rs (file reader), src/quant/ (dequantization), src/model.rs (CPU reference forward),
src/cuda/ and src/vulkan/ (GPU kernels, behind src/backend.rs), src/gpu_model.rs (GPU forward),
src/expert_cache.rs (expert placement), src/deepseek/, src/glm/, src/hy4/, src/inkling2/ and src/gemma4/
(the models with their own forward), src/serve.rs (HTTP), src/chat.rs (chat templates and tool calls),
src/main.rs (CLI).
RustingStrata is released under the RustingStrata License 1.0. You may use, modify and distribute it, including for commercial services, as long as you keep the license and credit Vasyl Trefilov as the original author. You may not sell RustingStrata itself.

report.summary: RustingStrata 1.4.0 is a pure-Rust GGUF inference engine that streams MoE experts between CPU and GPU so models larger than VRAM still run on 12 GB cards.
report.background: Most local LLM inference still runs through llama.cpp and its ggml core, which means a C/C++ toolchain, hand-tuned CUDA kernels, and a hard VRAM ceiling. Mixture-of-Experts models broke that ceiling in an interesting way: a 27 GB MoE file may only activate a small slice of its experts per token, so the rest can live in system RAM and be paged in on demand. ktransformers popularised this CPU-plus-GPU split for DeepSeek-class models, and llama.cpp added its own offload flags. RustingStrata attacks the same problem from a different angle: an entirely Rust codebase with no ggml dependency, GPU kernels written once and compiled at runtime through NVRTC on NVIDIA or run as-is on Vulkan, so users skip the CUDA SDK build step and the vendor lock-in that usually comes with it.
key_points: No ggml, no C++ build step. Kernels are compiled at runtime with NVRTC on NVIDIA hardware, and the same kernel source runs on Vulkan 1.3 (and experimentally ROCm/HIP via hiprtc). If NVRTC is missing, the engine silently falls back to Vulkan. The first CUDA run spends roughly 15 seconds compiling, then caches the result.

Experts that do not fit in VRAM run on the CPU at the same time as GPU work, and the placement adapts to the routing the model actually sees. Slot state that overflows VRAM stays in RAM. The demo: a 27 GB Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE file on a 12 GB RTX 3060, benchmarked against a tuned llama.cpp on the same file.

Batched parallel serving. serve --parallel N decodes concurrent requests in a single batched forward pass on CUDA, and each expert is read once per step for all requests, which is where the throughput gain over sequential serving comes from.

Broad architecture coverage: Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5/3.6, Gemma 4, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and others, several with their own dedicated forward implementations. Extras include an OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API, MCP tools, prompt caching, LoRA adapters, and a calibrate command that searches chunk size and draft settings per model and machine.

Easy distribution and an unusual licence. One-line installers for Windows and Linux, an AUR package, cargo build, and a self-update command. The RustingStrata License 1.0 permits commercial use and modification with attribution, but forbids reselling the software itself.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is another data point that the ggml monoculture is eroding: a single Rust codebase shipping CUDA, Vulkan and HIP backends from one kernel source undercuts the assumption that serious GPU inference requires a C++ build pipeline. Runtime kernel compilation also means new GPUs and new quantisation types can be supported without shipping prebuilt binaries per architecture. For developers, the appeal is practical: no CUDA toolkit install, a readable source map from gguf.rs through expert_cache.rs, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that drops into existing tooling. For regular users, the headline is economic: a 12 GB consumer card can host a 27 GB MoE model at usable speeds, which weakens the case for buying datacentre-class VRAM. The caveats are real, though. Numbers are self-reported against a tuned llama.cpp, the MoE column swings about 30 percent run to run, and vLLM comparisons are not like-for-like.
report.tools: Worth comparing against llama.cpp (the baseline it benchmarks against, with its own --n-cpu-moe offload), ktransformers (the original CPU+GPU MoE split for DeepSeek-class models), and vLLM for high-throughput serving when the model does fit in VRAM. For the Rust ecosystem, mistral.rs and candle are the natural neighbours. To try RustingStrata, grab a release binary or the one-line installer, then point Open WebUI, Jan or SillyTavern at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1. Read BENCHMARKS.md and SUPPORTED_GPUS.md before trusting the numbers.
